bio.en: Gaurav Misra is the co-founder and CEO of Captions, a leading consumer AI app for generating and editing talking videos with over 10 million users, and was previously an early employee at Snap who led its design engineering team.
bio.zh: Gaurav Misra 是 Captions 的联合创始人兼 CEO；Captions 是一款领先的消费级 AI 应用，可用 AI 生成和编辑口播视频，用户超 1000 万，他此前是 Snap 的早期员工并领导其设计工程团队。

summary.en: Gaurav walks through how a modern AI-native startup actually operates: every engineer ships a marketable product or feature every single week, they deliberately take on technical debt to move faster than big companies, and they run a hidden 'secret roadmap' alongside the public one because user-requested features are rarely a competitive edge. He reflects on what Snap taught him about building consumer/social apps—running with no PMs and letting designers run the show—and grapples with a world where AI-generated video is indistinguishable from real. The episode is packed with operating lessons for anyone building on top of AI.
summary.zh: Gaurav 拆解了一家现代 AI 原生创业公司的真实运作方式：每位工程师每周都要交付一个可上市的产品或功能；他们刻意承担技术债务，以比大公司更快的速度前进；并在公开路线图之外另设一条“秘密路线图”，因为用户提出的功能很少构成竞争优势。他回顾了 Snap 教给他的关于打造消费/社交应用的经验——不设 PM、由设计师主导，也直面了“AI 视频真假难辨”的世界。这期节目充满面向所有在 AI 之上构建产品者的运营经验。

turns.speaker: Gaurav Misra
turns.en: There's rarely a time like this where so much is possible. Even like five, seven years ago, it's so hard to start a company. Everything feels like it's done, someone else is working on it. Suddenly, it's a time, right now, which I've never even experienced, where everything you try just works.
turns.zh: 很少有像现在这样机遇遍布的时代。即便是在五年、七年前，要创办一家公司都困难重重。似乎所有领域都已被占据，别人早已在开发相关产品。然而当下却迎来了一个前所未有的黄金时期——你尝试的每件事似乎都能一击即中。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: With people constantly hearing about all the things happening. Is there any tools or processes or approaches you've figured out to help stay focused?

turns.speaker: Gaurav Misra
turns.en: Our engineering goal is every engineer should ship a marketable product every week.
turns.zh: 我们的工程目标是每位工程师每周都要交付一款可上市的产品。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love just how wild that sounds. How do you maintain quality and make it all cohesive?

turns.speaker: Gaurav Misra
turns.en: I actually think as a startup your job is to take on technical debt because that is how you operate faster than a bigger company. Bigger companies don't take contact technical debt, they pay it usually right away, or they're paying back technical debt from the days when they were a startup.
turns.zh: 我认为初创公司应该主动承担技术债务，因为这样才能比大公司更快地行动。大公司通常不会主动背负技术债务，而是会立即偿还债务，或者是在初创时期就已经积累了技术债务。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there anything else that in how you operate and the way you build product that you think is really unique and interesting?
turns.zh: 在运营和产品开发方面，有没有什么独特而有趣的做法？

turns.speaker: Gaurav Misra
turns.en: We have what we think of as the public roadmap. This is basically what people have asked us for. There's all these surface areas where we receive user feedback, but these are all features that every competitor knows about. If a user is asking us for it, they're asking everybody for it. (00:01:04): It's not going to be a game changer in terms of winning against your competition. So we have a second roadmap which we think of as a secret roadmap.
turns.zh: 我们制定了所谓的公开路线图。这基本上是用户向我们提出的需求。我们有很多收集用户反馈的渠道，但这些功能都是所有竞争对手都熟悉的。如果用户向我们提出这些需求，那其他公司也会收到同样的请求。（00:01:04）：这并不会成为你在竞争中脱颖而出的关键。因此，我们还有第二份路线图，我们称之为秘密路线图。

turns.speaker: Gaurav Misra
turns.en: Appreciate it. Honestly, it's an exciting time. I got to say like there's rarely a time like this where so much is possible. In normal times, if you think about even five, seven years ago, it's so hard to start a company. It's so hard to come up with an idea. It's just like everything feels like it's done, someone else is working on it. Or it's like, oh it's been tried three times and failed three times. And suddenly, it's a time, right now, which I've never even experienced honestly in my career, where everything you try just works. (00:05:56): There's so many possibilities. There's not enough people in the world to work on them. Honestly. There's more things that can be done than there's people available to do them. It is just such a rare thing. And honestly, it's not going to last forever. We are going to catch up to this, but just feels lucky to be part of that movement. It's awesome.
turns.zh: 非常感激。说实话，现在是个令人兴奋的时代。我得说，这样的充满无限可能的时刻实属难得。在正常时期，回想五年、七年前创业环境简直太难了。创意太难产生，感觉什么都被做过了，别人已经在做类似项目，或者某个想法尝试三次都失败了。而现在这个时代，我职业生涯中从未经历过——几乎每件事一试就成功。（00:05:56）：可能性太多了，但全球能干这事的人不够。说真的，能做的事远超能做事的人。这真是难得一遇的机会。不过好景不会长久，我们终会迎头赶上，但能成为这场变革的一份子，真的很幸运。太棒了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: When you said everything is working, I think what's an important distinction there is the building of the tool works. The tech is now there to build all these things that have not been possible before. The thing that is increasingly, difficult, and I want to get your take on this, is getting anyone to pay attention and stick with your thing because it's so easy to build stuff and everything is just awesome and interesting. It's harder to get people to pay attention and stick with your product. (00:06:42): So I guess is there anything there, you've learned that you've built a number of successful products. We'll talk about Snap and what you're doing now, about just, I don't know, what you need to think about these days to get anyone to pay attention and then stick around.
turns.zh: 您说一切都运作得很好，但这里有个重要的区别——工具的构建是可行的。现在有技术支持构建以前无法实现的项目。但越来越困难的是让用户关注并持续使用你的产品，因为现在开发东西太容易了，一切都充满吸引力和趣味性。要让用户关注并留存，挑战确实更大了。（00:06:42）：所以我想问问您，您构建过多个成功产品，有什么经验可以分享吗？我们会聊聊Snap和您现在在做的事，或者说您觉得当下要怎么做才能让用户关注并持续使用产品。

turns.speaker: Gaurav Misra
turns.en: Yeah, I mean honestly it's a great point and I think there is a lot of hype obviously, and part of it, that's what's driving a lot of this growth for a lot of companies. And I think from a user acquisition/marketing perspective, in a world five or seven years ago, if you were making something novel and you went to users and it was like, "Oh, we got something better." People are going to be like, "Well, whatever. Everybody says they got something better. I don't care." But today, and this is not probably the way you should do it, but you can go and just say, "We've rethought this thing with AI." And a bunch of people will just be like, "Well, how?" Or "Maybe I should check this out." (00:07:33): They'll just try it. Obviously, you have to deliver on the promises. If you don't deliver, people will come in, they'll play around a bunch and then just leave. But if you can truly deliver on the promises, there's great opportunities to require users at scale. So I think that's slightly different. And I don't know how long that lasts, but it is definitely a different time from that perspective. I do think also at the core of building products is solving problems. I think a lot of people sort of get caught up in this, well, it's cool and people will come for the cool right now. People will come in and be like, "Well, let me check it out. It's cool." (00:08:11): But at the end of the day, if you're just building a playground and people play around in the playground and then they leave after playing around, it's not a business. So I think that is still key. You have to be solving real problems.
turns.zh: 是啊，我说实话，这观点很棒。显然，现在确实有很多炒作，而这其中一部分也正是推动许多公司快速发展的动力。从用户获取和市场推广的角度来看，如果五年或七年前你做一个创新产品，然后对用户说：“哦，我们有更好的东西。” 人们可能会说：“嗯，随便吧。每个人都说自己有更好的东西，我才不在乎呢。” 但如今，你甚至可以直接说：“我们用AI重新构思了这个产品。” 一群人就会问：“哦，具体怎么做？” 或者“也许我该试试看。” （00:07:33）：他们就会尝试。当然，你得兑现承诺。如果做不到，人们来了玩一玩然后就走了。但如果你能真正兑现承诺，就有机会大规模获取用户。所以我觉得这点还是有点不同的。我不知道这种情况能持续多久，但从这个角度来看，现在确实是不同时代了。我确实认为产品开发的核心是解决问题。我觉得很多人都沉浸在这种思维里：哦，这个很酷，人们现在会为了酷而来。 （00:08:11）：但说到底，如果你只是建个游乐场，人们玩一玩然后就走了，这可不是生意。所以我觉得这点还是关键。你必须要解决真正的问题。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: As we were talking, I'm thinking about every day there's something that would maybe a few years ago be news for a year. Holy shit, this is now possible. Now it's like every day something like that happens and then we're like, all right, so what I think about is like, we'll have AGI one of these days or super intelligence and everyone's going to be, "Oh, amazing." And then, "Okay, what's for dinner?"
turns.zh: 我们聊天的时候，我就在想，几年前可能还会成为头条新闻的东西，现在每天都在发生。天啊，这现在都实现了。现在每天都有类似的事情发生，然后我们就想，嗯，那又怎样。我就会想，总有一天我们会拥有通用人工智能，或者超级智能，然后大家都会说：“哦，太棒了。” 然后问：“好吧，晚饭吃什么？”

turns.speaker: Gaurav Misra
turns.en: Isn't that already happening? Think about, in a way, I self-reflect on this sometimes if like, you've seen Iron Man and stuff, they have the J.A.R.V.I.S thing and you've seen Interstellar and they have the TARS machine. They're talking back and forth with these things like bouncing ideas. That is science fiction. That's literally science fiction. Okay, it's not perfect, but it exists in a way that nobody could have imagined. That's science fiction has become reality and I feel like nobody cares. (00:09:18): In a way, you would've expected the world to be turned upside down, but it feels like almost in a way so slow and people are like, yes, adoption is happening, but I feel like it's almost a shocking development in a way.
turns.zh:
这不已经在发生了吗？有时候我会自省，比如你看过《钢铁侠》之类的电影，他们有贾维斯这样的系统，还有《星际效应》里的塔尔斯机器。人们和这些东西对话、交流想法。这就是科幻。这简直就是科幻。好吧，它还不完美，但它以一种超乎想象的方式存在了。科幻已经成为现实，可惜没人太在意。
（00:09:18）：某种程度上，你可能会觉得世界应该天翻地覆，但感觉进展太慢了。人们会说，嗯，确实在普及，但我觉得这发展得太出乎意料了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It feels like you guys have done a good job staying top of mind and continuing to get people excited because to your point, there's so much happening. How do you get people to continue to be like, "Oh, okay, wow, what their building is actually is interesting and continues to be interesting." (00:09:45): Anything you've learned about just what it takes to stay top of mind and continue to pull people back and get people re-excited over and over?
turns.zh: 感觉你们在保持品牌曝光度方面做得很出色，持续激发人们的兴趣。正如你所说，现在确实有很多新鲜事物在发生。你们是如何让人们持续惊叹：“哦，原来他们在做这个，真有意思，而且一直这么有趣。”（00:09:45）：对于如何持续保持品牌曝光度、吸引用户并一次又一次激发他们的兴趣，你们有什么心得吗？

turns.speaker: Gaurav Misra
turns.en: Hundred percent. I mean, I think honestly it just comes down to not just AI for the sake of AI or AI for the sake of excitement or hype or novelty or whatever that is, it's actually effective AI like AI that solves real problems, practical problems. And the fundamentals haven't changed. In a way, there's three steps to building products. You identify a user problem, you apply some technology to solve that problem, but then finally you have some mechanism to find people who have that problem. If you can do all three of those things, then in any environment you can create great products. But I think right now what's different is so much is changing on the technology side that you can create products that could not have been created before and solve problems that could not have been solved before. And that's creating the opportunity. (00:10:45): And for us, especially in the video space, it's truly endless. We've just begun, our goal specifically for video is not to build professional tools. We're not building for professionals at all. We're building for the person who could not have created video before. They didn't have the tools, the skills, the means to be able to create video and now they can because they're able to jump over that skill gap or that time gap. Maybe they're business owners, they don't have time, they want results, and honestly a lot to solve there just tons.
turns.zh: 完全赞同。我觉得关键在于，不能为了AI而用AI，也不能为了制造轰动效应、炒作或猎奇而用AI。真正有效的AI应该能解决实际问题，比如实用性问题。基本原则从未改变。构建产品有三个步骤：识别用户痛点，应用技术解决问题，最后找到有此痛点的人群。如果能做好这三点，在任何环境下都能打造出优秀的产品。但当下不同的是，技术层面发生了巨大变革，让我们能创造出过去无法实现的产品，解决过去无法解决的问题。这才创造了机遇。（00:10:45）：对我们来说，尤其是在视频领域，机遇是无穷无尽的。我们才刚刚起步，视频业务的目标不是为专业人士打造工具。我们根本不针对专业人士，而是为那些过去无法创作视频的人服务。他们缺乏工具、技能和资源，现在却能跨越这些障碍。或许他们是忙碌的创业者，时间紧迫但渴望看到成果，这背后有太多亟待解决的问题。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Solve people's problems. Easier said than done, but it's a good reminder. In the end that's all that matters. Something that I always think about with people in your shoes is just how do you not get overwhelmed and how do you know what to pay attention to? How do you stay focused? (00:11:36): Any tips there for folks that are just reading every day, a new announcement, and then just like I just, how do I? What do I do? There's too much.
turns.zh: 解决用户痛点。说起来容易做起来难，但这提醒我们最重要的是什么。说到你们这种处境的人，我总会想，他们如何不被压得喘不过气？如何明确关注重点？（00:11:36）：对于每天浏览各种新公告、却感到无从下手的人，有什么建议吗？

turns.speaker: Gaurav Misra
turns.en: It is the new problem of product development in a way. There's too many possible paths you can go down. There's too many ideas, there's too many things you could do. And I mean obviously, prioritization is always an important skill set and has always been, but it's become an even more important skill set right now because you have to figure out what not to pay attention to. Our general framework for it is to look for user demand, and actually the easiest way to check for user demand is to just see what has virality. (00:12:10): Usually, what has virality and what people want to share and talk about, there's something at the core of it that actually is interesting. Now, it may not always be interesting in a way that's like maybe it's a one-time use case. Maybe it's not something that people would do repeatedly. Maybe it's not something you could build like a subscription business off of, but oftentimes there's some things, some core element of it that has resonated with people. And if you can identify that core and then mold it into fitting into your business, it's actually a great way to identify what actually works. And we have these tools right now. We don't have to build anything. You can just kind talk about it and people will share it, share the idea. (00:12:49): And you can measure how well the product might be received even before you built anything. So it's a great tool we use for prioritization. We spend a lot of time on social media. Obviously, our app is often used for social media, so a lot of our employees will spend a lot of time on social media. We look at what the trends are, what's happening, and based on that we can get a pretty good read of what might resonate well with people.
turns.zh: 某种程度上，这是产品开发面临的新挑战。可能的路径太多了，创意层出不穷，待做之事数不胜数。显然，优先排序始终是一项重要的技能，但如今它变得更为关键——因为你必须学会过滤掉不该关注的方向。我们通常的思路是洞察用户需求，而验证用户需求最简单的方法就是观察哪些内容容易传播。（00:12:10）通常，那些引发传播热潮、被人们分享和讨论的内容，其核心价值往往很有趣。当然，这种趣味性不一定体现在重复使用的场景中，也许并非人们会反复操作的功能，或是无法构建订阅商业模式的服务，但其核心元素总能引发共鸣。若能识别出这种核心价值并将其融入业务框架，就是找到有效方向的绝佳途径。如今我们已有成熟工具，无需另行开发。只需口头阐述创意，人们就会自发分享，助你提前评估产品接受度。这些工具是我们优先排序的利器。我们团队深耕社交媒体领域，应用本身也常用于社交场景。因此，许多员工会花大量时间研究社交趋势，基于这些洞察，我们能精准把握哪些创意最能引发用户共鸣。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So as a leader of a company with people constantly hearing about all the things happening, is there any tools or processes or approaches you've figured out to help people continue, stay focused, not get excited about every shiny new object and actually ship things? I
turns.zh: 那么，作为一家员工时刻接收海量信息的公司的领导者，您是否总结出过哪些工具、流程或方法，能帮助团队成员保持专注，抵制住对新奇事物的追逐，并最终把事情落到实处？

turns.speaker: Gaurav Misra
turns.en: I mean honestly, it's all about incrementality in a way. I think we do aim to ship every week. Our engineering goal is every engineer should ship a marketable product every week. And so what's a marketable product is a product that you can show to users and the user might subscribe or pay for the app just for that or come to the app essentially just for that. And that's why table stakes features, let's say we're talking about word processor or something. If you had auto format or just table stakes stuff like justify alignment or something, no one's going to come to your word processor for justify alignment. You can market that because it's obvious, of course it exists, but if you did something unique that nobody else has done, you can go and show that to people and people will come to your app just for that. (00:14:22): And even if your app doesn't have a lot of the obvious stuff, maybe it doesn't have justify alignment, people will jump over that just to use these new tools and new abilities that you might be building and marketing. So we try to do every engineer one marketable feature per week, and a lot of that stuff may not work, but a lot of it does work and we can figure out obviously, where to put in more effort, things that start to work, we double down on those things, build more. People often complain because think about it, in one week where we're shipping, it's not complete, it's MVP, truly. (00:14:57): And we slice the hell out of it. We take the design and we cut, cut, cut until we can really say that it's going to be useless if we cut anymore. We get that out and people come in. And if things are going well, people will use it despite all the problems that it might have, and now people will complain and we'll have a list of problems and we know what to do next. That's a starting point essentially. As long as we're shipping one a week, we get a ton of volume of features and products and directions we're releasing, cut a lot of that. What remains expand from there. So it works really well, and it keeps people focused.
turns.zh: 老实说，这在某种程度上就是关于增量改进的。我们确实致力于每周发布新功能。我们的工程目标是，每位工程师每周都要交付一个可市场化的产品。所谓可市场化的产品，就是能展示给用户的产品，用户可能会为此订阅或付费，或者专门为此访问应用。这就是为什么基础功能很重要。比如说我们讨论文字处理器之类的应用，如果只有自动格式化之类的基本功能，没有人会为了对齐文本之类的功能专门下载你的文字处理器。虽然这类功能显而易见，但如果你开发出独一无二的功能，人们就会为此访问你的应用。（00:14:22）即便你的应用缺少一些基础功能，比如对齐文本，人们也会为了使用你正在开发和推广的新工具而忽略这些不足。（00:14:57）我们要求每位工程师每周交付一个可市场化的功能，虽然很多功能可能失败，但很多确实成功了。对于成功的功能，我们会加倍投入，进一步开发。人们常抱怨说，因为我们每周发布的都是MVP级别的产品，功能不完整。（00:15:12）我们会对设计进行精简，砍掉不必要的部分，直到砍到再删减就毫无意义了。然后上线后，用户即使发现问题也会使用，再根据反馈列出问题清单，确定下一步方向。这基本上就是起点。只要我们每周都能发布新功能，我们就能积累大量产品方向和功能，进行筛选，剩下的再拓展。这套方法效果显著，能让团队保持专注。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love the simplicity of that. I love just how wild that sounds for a lot of companies I imagine. Every engineer ships a marketable feature or product every week.
turns.zh: 我喜欢这种简单直接。我能想象对很多公司来说，这听起来太疯狂了。每个工程师每周都要交付一个可市场化的功能或产品。

turns.speaker: Gaurav Misra
turns.en: Yes.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: There's some people listening to this and are just completely stressed out by this idea and there's some people listening who are like, this is exactly how I want to work. This is how every company should build.
turns.zh: 有些听众听了这个想法会感到压力巨大，而有些听众则会觉得这正是他们理想的工作方式，每家公司都应该这样做。

turns.speaker: Gaurav Misra
turns.en: Yep.
turns.zh: 没错。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: How do you maintain quality and make it all cohesive? I imagine that's the big trade-off. Just, any tricks there for folks that want to maybe start operating this way.
turns.zh: 如何保证质量并让一切协调一致？我觉得这是一个巨大的平衡。那么，对于那些想尝试这种工作方式的人，有什么技巧可以分享吗？

turns.speaker: Gaurav Misra
turns.en: Quality is not something you compromise on most of the time. I think yes, there's strategic compromises in quality, but most of the time what you want to do is have a bar for quality where people should come in and if they're using the feature, it should work, right? Of course. And the way to cut down on time, and I think this is a mistake people make a lot of the time, is when time is being pressured downward, a lot of times engineers, PMS, designers, they will cut on quality rather than cutting on scope. And actually you can cut on scope. It's actually, the method that we use is we look at every element that's going to take any time to build and we just say, what if we remove this? Is the product still useful? (00:16:48): And we keep repeating that until we remove whatever's left and we say it's going to be useless at this point. And that becomes the one-week project, right? It actually really works. It narrows down to the core of what you're really trying to ask. So for example, let's say we wanted to build something to add an image on your video or something like that, and this is a really basic idea. I just made it up right now. And you might imagine a design in which you import your image from your camera roll, but before it lands in your video you might want to remove the background. You might want to change the hue and saturation or something like that. And you might expect a designer to design all of those features and you let it design, but you really quickly realize that you can cut all of that stuff. (00:17:38): You can cut the background or you can cut the hue saturation. All you really need is pick. And then there might be a picker. We need a picker with a library, with a lot of different type. What if you want to pull from the cloud? What if you want to pull from the drive or something like that? Cut all of that, right? And essentially come down to the core, which is just native picker from the camera, lens, straight in the video, no UI. And that is already, that should be useful. If that's not useful, then anything else built on top of that is also useless. So that's how we might go about it.
turns.zh: 质量绝大多数时候都不是可以妥协的。我认为确实存在战略性的质量妥协，但大多数时候你的目标应该是设定一个质量标准，让用户使用产品时它必须能正常运行，对吧？当然没错。而缩短开发周期（我觉得这也是人们常犯的错误）的方法是，当时间紧迫时，工程师、产品经理和设计师往往会削减质量而非缩减功能范围。实际上你完全可以削减功能范围。我们的做法是，审视每个需要耗费时间开发的元素，然后问：如果去掉它，产品还能用吗？（00:16:48）我们不断重复这个过程，直到剩下最后一个功能时，发现它已然毫无用处。这时候它就成了为期一周的项目，对吧？这种方法确实有效，能直击核心需求。比如说，假设我们想开发一个能在视频上添加图片的功能（这只是个很简单的想法，我刚想出来的）。你可能会设想这样的设计流程：从相册导入图片，然后在放入视频前去除背景，调整色调和饱和度之类的。你可能会以为需要设计师把这些功能都设计出来再实现，但很快你就会发现完全没必要。（00:17:38）你可以去掉背景，去掉色调和饱和度。你真正需要的只是一个图片选择器。那么需要一个带有大量不同类型图片的选择器库。如果想从云端获取图片呢？如果想从本地驱动器获取呢？把这些都去掉。最终归结到核心需求——直接从相机、镜头获取原始图片，完全不需要界面。如果这个功能没用，那基于它构建的任何东西也都没用。所以这就是我们的思路。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That last sentence is so key to this. It's the core idea of ship small iterative features before you invest a lot in something to figure out is there anything there, is this worth spending weeks on?
turns.zh: 最后这句话太关键了。这是核心理念：在投入大量资源之前，先快速推出小型迭代功能，验证是否有市场需求，是否值得花几周时间去打磨。

turns.speaker: Gaurav Misra
turns.en: Totally. And I think the coolest part of this method is the first thing that the users will come in, they'll use the thing, they'll import images and the first thing they'll complain about is what bothers them the most? Is it human saturation? Is it background removal? Is it picking from the cloud? You'll just get the most complaints about that thing. (00:18:43): People will be like, and people will be honest about it or they'll be like, "This sucks. It doesn't even have background removal. What kind of image thing is this?" And you have to take that feedback and just next week you can ship in a single week all the things that the user's complaining about.
turns.zh: 完全正确。我认为这种方法最酷的地方在于，用户刚开始使用时，会导入图片，然后他们抱怨最多的是什么？是人脸识别饱和问题？是背景去除功能？还是云端选图功能？这些问题会引发最多的抱怨。（00:18:43）：用户会说，或者他们会坦诚地说：“这太糟糕了。连背景去除功能都没有，这算什么图片处理工具？”你必须认真对待这些反馈，下周就能把用户抱怨的所有功能都改进上线。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And then they're like, wow, this team is shipping like crazy.
turns.zh: 然后他们会惊叹：哇，这个团队真是高效得令人惊叹。

turns.speaker: Gaurav Misra
turns.en: Yes. Exactly.
turns.zh: 没错。完全正确。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Solve all my problems. So responsive. This connects a common sign of product market fit, which is when people are complaining about the thing that means they actually care enough to complain and that's a really good sign if they're complaining about something.
turns.zh: 解决了我所有的问题。响应如此迅速。这揭示了产品市场匹配的一个常见迹象——当人们抱怨某个功能时，意味着他们足够在意去抱怨，这确实是个好兆头。

turns.speaker: Gaurav Misra
turns.en: It's very true, very true. If nobody complains, it's almost red flag.
turns.zh: 确实如此，确实如此。如果没人抱怨，那几乎是个危险信号。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: A lot of this is turning into an archeology of a modern product team and startup. So I want to keep digging. This is not where I was planning to go, but this is awesome. I love that this approach of every engineer shipping something every week that's marketable connects directly to where I started this conversation, which is how do you stay above the noise? (00:19:36): And part of the answer is just ship stuff constantly, and just continue to impress people. Like, "Here's a new amazing video feature." "Look at this thing."
turns.zh: 这部分内容逐渐演变成对现代产品团队和初创公司的考古研究。所以我想要继续深挖。这并非我原本的计划，但这太棒了。我喜欢这种每个工程师每周都发布可市场化的功能的做法，这直接与我开启这场对话的初衷相契合——如何在喧嚣中脱颖而出？（00:19:36）：部分答案就是持续快速发布产品，不断给人惊喜。比如：“这里有个新的惊艳视频功能。”“看看这个东西。”

turns.speaker: Gaurav Misra
turns.en: Exactly. Yep. I think it's definitely key, right? And there's enough area and enough scope for that to happen. I think truly in normal times it may not be possible to create that much roadmap that quickly, but I think because there's so much innovation underlying all this, there is that scope available. The roadmap almost seems unlimited, just truly.
turns.zh: 完全正确。没错。我认为这绝对关键，对吧？而且有足够的空间和机会去实现这一点。正常情况下，可能无法如此快速地制定如此详尽的路线图，但鉴于这背后有如此多的创新，确实有这样的可能性。这份路线图几乎是无限的，真的就是这样。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. The other question I imagine people would be wondering is how do you work on longer-term projects that take many weeks? There's also infrastructure, I guess, back-end stuff. So maybe answer those questions. (00:20:17): How do you think about long-term stuff and then how do you deal with back-end stuff that isn't a feature that anyone would care for?
turns.zh: 好的。我想观众可能还想知道，如何处理需要数周时间的长期项目？还有基础设施，应该是后端部分吧。或许可以回答一下这些问题。（00:20:17）：你如何看待长期项目，又如何处理没人关心的后端功能？

turns.speaker: Gaurav Misra
turns.en: Yep. Usually, we'll dedicate time to that separately. For example, usually Q4 for us is infrastructure quarter. We just go and build all the infrastructure. Q4 is generally, we've already delivered a ton of products and stuff. We're feeling pretty good about the rest of the year. Things are winding down. Obviously, holidays and stuff coming up. And so we spend all that time paying the technical debt. (00:20:48): I actually think there's a unique thing to think here about technical debt in general. And as a startup, your job is to take on technical debt because that is how you operate faster than a bigger company. Bigger companies don't take on technical debt, they pay it usually right away. Or they're paying back technical debt from the days when they were a startup, and they took on a lot of it. I mean Snaps, I used to work at Snap and there was a lot of examples of that over there, and I'm sure it happens at every other company. (00:21:19): And we think about it as like, well, is this a problem we need to solve today or is this a problem that the 50th engineer or the hundredth engineer or the 500th engineer can solve? And if it is a problem that a future engineer can solve, we should use that future engineer now. Essentially, that's what we're doing. And we're saying we're going to push this to somebody in the future. And by the way, if the company fails, that engineer will never be hired and all this won't matter anyways. So it's like financial debt in many ways. Financial debt is taken on to create leverage. It can be a good thing like if you're buying a house, you take on debt and you can buy something probably more than you can afford without taking on debt. (00:22:04): And it's the same thing. You can create products that you wouldn't be able to build with a small team that you have by taking on strategic technical debt. It's very positive actually.
turns.zh: 是的。通常，我们会专门为此留出时间。比如，对我们来说，第四季度通常是基础设施建设季。我们会集中精力搭建所有基础设施。第四季度通常意味着我们已经推出了大量产品，业务进展顺利，年底收尾工作也接近尾声。当然，假期临近，各种事务逐渐增多。所以我们会把所有时间用来偿还技术债务。（00:20:48）：我认为关于技术债务，有一点值得深思。作为初创公司，你的职责就是主动承担技术债务，因为这能让你比大公司运作得更快。大公司通常不愿意承担技术债务，而是会立即偿还。或者说，他们是在偿还初创时期积累的技术债务。我在Snap工作过，那里有很多这样的例子，我相信其他公司也一样。（00:21:19）：我们会这样考虑：这个问题是我们今天必须解决的，还是留给第50位、第100位、第500位工程师去处理的？如果是未来工程师能解决的问题，我们现在就应该启用他们。本质上，我们就是这么做的。我们说要把问题推给未来的人。但如果公司倒闭了，那位工程师也永远不会被录用，所有努力都白费了。这在很多方面就像财务债务。财务债务是为了创造杠杆而承担的。比如买房时，借债就能买到超出自己承受能力的房子。（00:22:04）：道理是一样的。通过承担战略性技术债务，你能用现有的小团队打造出原本无法完成的产品。这实际上是件好事。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow, this is such a cool idea. And where my mind goes is that future engineer may be an AI agent engineer.
turns.zh: 哇，这真是个很棒的想法。我突然想到，未来的工程师可能是人工智能工程师。

turns.speaker: Gaurav Misra
turns.en: Exactly, yeah.
turns.zh: 对啊。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Just solving problems, just on technical debt in you.
turns.zh: 就是专注于解决技术债务。

turns.speaker: Gaurav Misra
turns.en: Exactly. Some engineer in the future Five-hundred engineer many years from now will get a promotion because they solve this big problem that those really bad early engineers created.
turns.zh: 没错。未来的工程师，比如五百年后的工程师，可能会因为解决了那些早期糟糕工程师制造的大问题而获得晋升。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So obviously, there's a line to this. There's only so much debt you can take on before you become a big problem. (00:22:43): Is there any thoughts on just that balance of just how much is too much and how if it's enough for a net feature engineer or just-
turns.zh: 显然，这里面有个界限。技术债务积累到一定程度就会成为大问题了。（00:22:43）：对于技术债务的平衡，有没有什么思考，比如多少算过度？对于净功能工程师来说，又该如何判断？

turns.speaker: Gaurav Misra
turns.en: Yeah, I mean I think generally the rule of thumb is every piece of debt that you take on you have to pay interest on. So if there is debt that you've taken on, there's 1% or 2% of your time that is going to be taken away every day in maintaining bugs and issues and restarts and crashes and things that are happening with that. Because you did it the fast way, something's going to go wrong with it. Every day. 1% of your time will be taken away. If you take on enough debt, you'll be paying 80 or 90% interest and you'll not have any time to do anything new. You'll just be paying interest. That's all. (00:23:23): And that's when you get into the mode of like, oh, we're just keeping the lights on. We don't have any engineers to do anything. We're just keeping the lights on. That's the failure case for a startup. So in a way, you have a technical debt runway. Once you run out, once you've taken on too much debt. And if you haven't delivered value in that time, enough value to hire the engineers to pay the interest or just pay off the debt, you'll get in trouble.
turns.zh: 是啊，我觉得一般来说，每个你承担的债务都需要支付利息。所以如果你背负了债务，每天就会有1%或2%的时间被用于处理各种漏洞、问题、重启、崩溃以及相关事务。因为你选择了快速上线的方式，总会有问题出现。每天都会占用你1%的时间。如果你背负的债务过多，支付的利息可能高达80%或90%，最终你就没时间做新的事情了。你只能一直还利息。这就是创业公司的失败模式。所以从某种程度上说，你有技术债务的“燃料储备”。一旦用完了，一旦债务过高，如果你在这段时间内没有创造足够的价值来雇佣工程师还利息或偿还债务，你就会陷入困境。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that. That's such a nice heuristic of how to think about when to invest in something. I don't want to go down this too far, but just a thought I have is ... because sometimes there's big technical decisions you got to make that impact the way everything builds or is built in the future. I imagine those you spend more time on and take really seriously.
turns.zh: 我喜欢这个观点。这是思考何时该投资某项事物的绝佳启发。我不想深入探讨，但我有个想法……因为有时你必须做出重大技术决策，这些决策会影响未来所有产品的构建方式。我想你会花更多时间在这些决策上，并非常认真地对待它们。

turns.speaker: Gaurav Misra
turns.en: Definitely. Yeah, I mean I think as long as it's possible for wherever it's like a two-way door, you can do whatever you want. I mean this is a classic methodology. If it's A one-way door, it's worth thinking about and sort of doing correctly at least as much as the one-way door would matter to you in the future.
turns.zh: 确实。我觉得只要有可能，只要这是一条双向门，你想怎么做都可以。我觉得这是一种经典的方法论。如果是单向门，那就值得思考和正确实施，至少要像单向门对你的未来那么重要。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: How much do your engineers use Cursor and tools like that to build? How much is AI helping your team move?
turns.zh: 你们的工程师使用Cursor和类似工具来开发的频率有多高？人工智能在帮助你们团队推进方面起到了多大作用？

turns.speaker: Gaurav Misra
turns.en: A hundred percent, yeah. I mean everybody's using it. It's super helpful. I mean even I'm using it honestly. Yeah, it's a huge multiplier for the team, no doubt.
turns.zh: 百分之百会用，是的。我觉得每个人都在用。这超级有帮助。说实话，我自己也在用。对团队来说绝对是个巨大的助力，这毫无疑问。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And is a Cursor specifically. Is there anything else that you guys found useful?
turns.zh: 特别是Cursor吗？你们还发现了其他有用的工具吗？

turns.speaker: Gaurav Misra
turns.en: Yeah, we are using Cursor. Yep. We've tried all the different tools. We were using Devin as well, which is another, you know? That's more advanced, I guess. It's solving bugs for you.
turns.zh: 是的，我们在用Cursor。没错。我们试用了各种工具，还用过Devin，这也是个更高级的工具。它能帮你排除漏洞。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, Devin's basically, I think it's 500 bucks a month and it's like an AI engineer that you just chat within Slack.
turns.zh: 是的，Devin基本上就是每月500美元，相当于一个你可以在Slack上直接聊天的人工智能工程师。

turns.speaker: Gaurav Misra
turns.en: Exactly, yeah. In a way, these are the types of things that us as a startup can do that bigger companies can't just, you know, they can't just pull in Devin. They have to get 30 lawyers in the room first before that happens.
turns.zh: 没错，确实是这样。从某种角度来看，这些正是我们初创公司能够做到而大公司无法做到的事情。比如，他们没法直接把德文招进来——要实现这个目标，他们得先召集30位律师开会讨论。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And they're all called Devin, these are like agents. Everyone's going to have hundreds of Devins working at their company.
turns.zh: 而且这些人都叫德文，听起来像是代理商。每个公司都会有数百个德文在为他们工作。

turns.speaker: Gaurav Misra
turns.en: Exactly. You can have multiple Devins. I actually heard you can have a manager of Devins who's managing Devins.
turns.zh: 没错，你甚至可以有多个德文。我听说还有专门管理德文的经理，负责协调各德文的工作。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that managers are all getting layered, like unlayered and then they're going to have AI managers. That's the ultimate bait and switch.
turns.zh: 我特别喜欢这种层层加码的管理模式——先是去层化，然后又引入AI经理。这简直就是最终的诱饵换鱼钩的把戏。

turns.speaker: Gaurav Misra
turns.en: Yep.
turns.zh: 是啊。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. Is there anything else that in how you operate and build the way you build product or set up the way you build product that you think is really unique and interesting that other people might be able to learn from?
turns.zh: 好的。在产品开发、构建流程或团队组建方面，有没有什么独特而有趣的做法，是其他人或许能借鉴学习的？

turns.speaker: Gaurav Misra
turns.en: Our process is a bit interesting in that way. We have a design team, we have a PM team. We're very early on those teams right now. And obviously, we have engineering. And we have all the different surface areas. So iOS, Android, web. There's backend team, machine learning team, research team. So generally, when we're developing products, we may start off with a PM first approach where we're finding some sort of overall issue that we want to take on some new area or pillar we want to take on and then creating sort of product specs from there. (00:26:17): But a lot of times we'll also start the opposite way. We'll first design something without even having any idea of what or why we're doing it, but we'll design a bunch of different things and then we'll sit down with the PMs and look at the designs and just go over one and the next and the next until we find interesting things and ideas that pop out of that. (00:26:36): And a lot of times that leads to us discovering things that we wouldn't have discovered if we were just too focused on the metrics and the numbers and things like that. So it's almost reversing the process a little bit and starting with design first, but it can often result in finding unique ideas basically. I also think that we have a unique setup in how we create our roadmap. So normally you have a single roadmap and we actually divide a roadmap into two different roadmaps. So we have what we think of as the public roadmap. This is basically what people have asked us for. So there's all these surface areas where we receive user feedback and we look at all that feedback and people will ask for features. They'll ask for, I want background removal, I want to undo and redo, I want to upload longer videos, whatever it is, a bunch of different features. (00:27:26): And we'll just make a list of that. And just like anything else, we'll prioritize it and we'll look at how many people it affects and what the possible markets are and just get it done basically one at a time. (00:27:37): But these are all features that every competitor knows about. These are public. If a user's asking us for it, they're asking everybody for it. And every team has essentially more or less the same list and everybody's prioritizing it. And yeah, sure you can win a little by extra nicely prioritizing it or winning a little in prioritization or execution or something, but it's not going to be a game changer in terms of winning against your competition. So we have a second roadmap which we think of as a secret roadmap. So this is a roadmap that nobody asked for anything on this like literally, nobody has ever asked for it. (00:28:13): And if a user were shown something on it, they might be like, "I don't need this. I don't know what this is." But given our unique vantage point, our unique understanding of the problem set, the user space and the technology, we've come up with some special ideas that we think will completely revolutionize how something is used where we can truly change the behavior of the user. I think that's what at is at the core of. It's like people are doing things one way if we're able to show them another way. And once they try it, they never go back. That's what a product is, that's success. And those are the types of ideas that we put on the secret roadmap. These are things we never talk about publicly, never tell anybody about, and we announce them and just give them to users and see the effects. (00:29:00): A lot of this we come up with through brainstorming. So we do actually do quarterly brainstorming, company-wide, everybody's included like everybody from. It's not just a product team thing, it's like engineering, recruiting, everybody's included in. And we all come up with marketing, obviously, everybody comes up with ideas, we vote on the ideas, rank the ideas, and then the product team takes over from there and thinks about like feasibility and technology and what the different things could be. So this is a way where we can take all that noise that people are getting, everybody's browsing social media, seeing all these different things that are blowing up, these models and advancements and we can get all that information together and provide a unique internal roadmap where how are we going to approach and create value out of all of these different advances that are happening. (00:29:49): So that's our general methodology. And a lot of times the biggest wins will come from the secret roadmap. That's the game-changing stuff. It's not going to be the user requests usually that are going to do that.
turns.zh:
我们的开发流程在这方面颇具趣味性。我们有设计团队和产品经理团队，目前这两个团队还处于早期阶段。当然，还有工程团队以及涵盖iOS、安卓、网页等各个领域的团队。此外，后端团队、机器学习团队和研究团队也一应俱全。通常来说，我们开发产品时，可能会先从产品经理的角度出发，寻找某个需要突破的新领域或核心支柱，然后据此制定产品规格。（00:26:17）但很多时候，我们也会反其道而行之。先设计出一些方案，哪怕当时还不知道为什么要这么做、要解决什么问题，但通过不断尝试不同设计，再与产品经理一起逐一评估，最终总能从中发现有趣的创意和思路。（00:26:36）这种方式常能让我们发现那些仅凭关注数据指标和数字无法发现的洞见。可以说，我们将流程稍作反转，先从设计入手，但最终往往能催生独特的创意。我认为我们在路线图制定方面也有独特的安排。通常一个公司只有一份路线图，而我们却将其拆分为两份。第一份是公开路线图，包含用户反馈的所有需求。比如，用户会提出背景去除、撤销重做、上传更长视频等各种功能需求。（00:27:26）我们会把这些需求列出来，然后按照优先级排序，考量影响人数和潜在市场，最终逐一实现。但这些功能竞争对手都已知晓，属于公开信息。如果用户向我们提出这些需求，说明其他公司也在追赶。各团队的优先级列表大同小异，执行力差异也微乎其微。因此，光靠在优先级或执行力上略胜一筹，根本无法在竞争中占据决定性优势。第二份路线图被我们称为秘密路线图，里面都是无人提及的创新构想。即便向用户展示这些功能，他们也会一头雾水。但凭借我们对用户场景、技术壁垒的独特洞察力，我们开发了诸多颠覆性创新方案，必将重塑用户体验。
正是在这里，我们能够真正改变用户的行为。我认为这才是问题的核心所在。比如说，如果我们能向人们展示另一种做事方式，他们原本可能一直沿用某种模式。而一旦他们尝试过新方法，就再也回不去了。这就是产品的本质，也是成功的秘诀。这些创意都被我们列入了秘密路线图——它们从不公开讨论，从不向外界透露。我们直接向用户发布，然后观察效果。

（00:29:00）：很多想法都是在头脑风暴中产生的。我们每季度都会举办全公司范围的头脑风暴会，所有人都能参与——不只是产品团队，工程、招聘等部门也都参与其中。大家会提出营销方面的想法，然后进行投票、排序。之后，产品团队会接手评估可行性、技术实现性，并构思具体方案。

（00:29:49）：我们会收集用户反馈，分析社交媒体上的热点内容、创新模式和技术进展，最终形成独家的内部路线图，指导我们如何从这些变革中创造价值。这就是我们的核心方法论。很多突破性成果往往来自秘密路线图——这些才是能改变游戏规则的创新成果，而用户需求反馈通常无法实现这种突破。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love just how calling it the secret roadmap makes it extra interesting. [inaudible 00:30:07]
turns.zh: 我特别喜欢把它称为"秘密路线图"，这样做就更增添了趣味性。 [00:30:07不可听清]

turns.speaker: Gaurav Misra
turns.en: Exactly, yeah. It's a secret.
turns.zh: 没错，确实是个秘密。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's a secret. I'm not even going to ask you what's on that secret roadmap. You can't tell me. (00:30:15): What's an example of feature that came out of that secret roadmap that's been a big deal for you guys?
turns.zh: 这确实是个秘密。我甚至都不会问你那份秘密路线图里有什么内容。你也不能告诉我。（00:30:15）：能举个例子，说明从那份秘密路线图中诞生的、对你们团队来说意义重大的功能吗？

turns.speaker: Gaurav Misra
turns.en: Tons. I mean, I'll give you an example from a long time ago. One of the first AI features we added after the app initially took off was this feature called eye contact. So this was a feature where if you're recording something, oftentimes people who are new to recording a video might read from a script or a teleprompter or something like that and they might have that off-screen. So it looks like you're reading and it's not great from the perspective of the video itself or the viewer of the video. So we had this feature where it basically shifts your eyes to look at the camera. (00:30:52): And we were actually the first company to build this. We worked with Nvidia on this. It's actually really interesting because when we originally reached out to Nvidia about this. They were not sure why we needed this. And they actually gave it to us pretty openly and were excited about some sort of partnership of how can we get this technology into something that could be useful. (00:31:19): But we saw this creator use case which was unique, and it was one of the ideas that came out of the brainstorm and we threw it on there, we launched it. It was a huge success. I mean, I'll be honest, the video, the ad that we made, a social media post that demonstrates this was so viral, it was made in basically every language around the world. It still till today gets millions of views. We find reposts and reposts of that thing that other people have created that get millions and millions and millions of views because people are like, "Wow, this is a great idea." (00:31:59): And now it's been copied the hell out of, I think it's available basically on every app you can imagine. For good reason of course. But that's one of the ideas that came out of it.
turns.zh: 太多了。我可以举个很久以前的例子。我们应用最初火起来后，添加的首批AI功能之一就是"目光接触"功能。当时用户录制视频时，常会对着脚本或提词器读台词，这样观众看视频时会觉得很不自然。所以我们开发了这个功能，能让用户在录制时把目光转向镜头。（00:30:52）：实际上，我们是首家开发这项技术的公司。我们与英伟达合作开发了这个功能。说起来挺有趣的，最初我们向英伟达介绍这个功能时，他们不明白我们为什么需要它。但他们非常开放地把技术分享给我们，并对可能的合作充满热情。（00:31:19）：但我们发现了一个独特的创作者场景用例，这是头脑风暴中诞生的创意之一。我们把它加入产品并上线了，反响非常好。说实话，我们制作的相关视频、广告和社交媒体帖子在全球多个语言版本都爆火了。直到现在仍有数百万的浏览量。我们能看到其他人转发的版本，也获得了数百万次的浏览量，因为人们都惊叹道："哇，这真是个好主意！"（00:31:59）：现在这个功能被疯狂模仿，几乎在你能想到的所有应用中都能看到。当然这是有充分理由的。但这就是从中诞生的创意之一。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You talked about how you come up with these secret roadmap ideas. I'm just intrigued by this. I'm going to spend a little more time here. (00:32:14): Does your team ever work with an AI LLM to help brainstorm? I imagine that's where things will go, where you're actually jamming. The AI agent is brainstorming along with you.
turns.zh: 你提到如何构思这些秘密路线图的创意。我对此很感兴趣，我想多花点时间探讨一下。（00:32:14）：你们团队是否会借助AI LLM来辅助头脑风暴？我猜这应该是创意涌现的过程，AI代理会和你一起头脑风暴。

turns.speaker: Gaurav Misra
turns.en: Honestly, I would like for it to go there. It hasn't gone there yet. We haven't done that exactly, because the problem is context. And I think just the context of understanding the user, the use case, it's so abstract. Even right now, I feel like I understand our users obviously, but I can't exactly verbalize why that is or how that is, a little bit abstract. And I spend a lot of time with RPMs and designers imparting anything that I understand and I've learned over the many years I've been working on this, how do I impart this to them? But then it's a challenge because I can't even verbalize it myself. And so it's an extra hard challenge to figure out how do I put this context? How do I make it available to an LLM when I can't even put it into words exactly. And honestly, this is probably my own feeling but, and I need to work on this, but there is something to it. (00:33:26): I do remember at Snap for example, I think one of the most unique things about Snap and the CEO Evan Spiegel was that he had an unmatched understanding of the user. I think years and years and years of the company's existence past, almost a decade. And nobody understood the user like he did. He would come up with ideas that everybody would disagree with and we would launch them and there would be hits, just hits after hits. And nobody would understand why. Everyone would line up and be like, "Great." Round of applause for everyone, but no one knew why. (00:34:07): A great example of that is a lot of this was figured out in retrospect too. I think there was a point at which Snap declared that they're a camera company and a lot of people laugh at them and said, "Camera. What are we making digital cameras or something?" Or, "Why is it a camera company?" (00:34:22): But I think at the core of it was this idea that Snapchat opens to the camera and that was actually the differentiator. That actually that small decision was holding the entire company against all competition because when the moment passes where your friend is doing something funny and you need to capture it, you're not going to open Instagram or anything else because it doesn't open to the camera. You're going to open Snapchat because you can capture it right away. And Instagram can never copy that because all their metrics are going to go down as soon as they do that. So that is a fundamental understanding. And I figured this out much later, actually, but it's such a powerful idea.
turns.zh: 老实说，我希望它能实现。但目前还没做到这一点。我们没能完全做到这一点，因为关键在于上下文。理解用户和用例的背景实在太抽象了。即便现在，我也觉得自己很清楚我们的用户，但我无法准确说清原因和具体方式，这有点抽象。我花了很多时间与产品经理和设计师交流，分享我多年积累的经验，但要把这些理解传达给他们实在是个挑战，因为我自己都难以用言语准确表达。如何把这种上下文呈现出来？当我连自己都无法清晰表达时，要让LLM理解更是难上加难。说实话，这可能只是我个人的感受，但我需要改进。（00:33:26）：我记得在Snap公司，埃文·斯皮格尔（Evan Spiegel）CEO最独特的地方在于他对用户有着无与伦比的理解。历经数年、近十年的发展历程，没有人比他更懂用户。他提出的很多想法都会遭到质疑，但一旦上线就能大获成功。大家都不明白其中的奥秘，只是附和说“不错”。（00:34:07）：很多东西都是事后才想明白的。Snap曾宣称自己是一家相机公司，当时很多人嘲笑他们：“相机？你们是做数码相机吗？”或者“为什么定位成相机公司？”但核心理念在于Snapchat能直接调用相机功能，这正是其核心竞争力。当朋友做趣事而你需要记录时，用户不会去打开Instagram或其他应用，因为它们无法快速调用相机功能，而是会选择Snapchat。Instagram永远无法复制这种体验，因为一旦模仿，用户数据必将下滑。这就是核心洞察。其实我很晚才领悟到这一点，但这个理念实在太有力量了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I'm glad you talked about Snap. That's where I definitely wanted to go. This is where I was going to start. So I'm glad we circled back to your experience at Snap. So the reason I am interested in this is if you think about social networks like Snap is basically the last social network to have launched and stuck around other than TikTok, which I don't think is a social network. I think it's just this content platform. I don't think you're really interacting with people really. And that was 2011 when it launched. So it's been like 15 years since the last social network launch that has worked. (00:35:40): And I think it's interesting also because there's rarely been a lot of insight into just how Snap operates. You were there really early. You're a big deal at Snap. You built a lot of really important features. So I wanted to spend a little time here, and it feels like a lot of things you learn from Snap you're bringing to your company now. So let me just ask, I think you may have answered this, but I'm curious if there's something else here just broadly maybe other than Ev's brain, what do you think was core to Snap being a successful consumer social product?
turns.zh:
很高兴你提到了Snap。这正是我最想探讨的领域，也是我最初的切入点。所以很高兴我们又回到了你对Snap的经验分享。之所以我对这家公司感兴趣，是因为你会发现，像Snap这样的社交平台，基本上是除TikTok之外最后一个成功立足的社交网络——但我个人认为TikTok不算社交网络，它更像是一个内容平台。用户在那里并没有真正与他人互动。Snap于2011年推出。距离上一个成功的社交网络问世，已经过去了整整15年。

另外，我觉得这个话题很有意思，因为外界对Snap的运营模式知之甚少。你很早就加入了Snap，在那里发挥了重要作用，开发了许多核心功能。所以我想多聊聊这部分。感觉你从Snap学到的很多东西，如今都应用到了自己的公司中。那么我想问，你可能已经回答过这个问题，但我很好奇，除了埃文（Ev）的卓越领导力外，你认为Snap成功成为消费级社交产品的核心要素还有哪些？

turns.speaker: Gaurav Misra
turns.en: There were a couple of different things that went well. I do think for a company like Snapchat or Social Network, the core product market fit can be extremely strong. Essentially, the reason that people are downloading it, the way that it's spreading, the way that it's distributing, the way that it's inviting friends or sending Snaps or whatever it is, that product market fit can be so strong sometimes that it can be hard to actually build something because you actually can't tell if what you're building is what's responsible for growing the thing or if it's actually hurting it and it's growing despite what you're doing basically. (00:36:53): And I think because of that, it actually sometimes teaches people the wrong things. It teaches people that the contrarian thing that they were doing was right when it was actually just wrong and the company just grew despite it. And I think some of the things that Snap did well and it needed to do really was to continue innovating, right? (00:37:17): Because for a company like Snap, it has a ton of competition. Social networks are monopolies by nature and there's a lot of reasons for Facebook or any other social network to stop the growth of Snapchat. And they tried, they tried really, really hard. And the way that Snap was avoiding that was by innovating. I think the core of it was the setup that they had, which was very unique. I've never seen anything like it. I've worked at a bunch of different companies, but obviously there's a CEO and the CEO was very product-led, his designer himself, but he surrounded himself with the design team. That was sort of the central team in the company. And the design team was like 10, 12 people. Basically, pretty small, even at 5, 6,000 employees it was that small still.
turns.zh: 有一几方面进展得还不错。我确实认为，对于像Snapchat这样的社交网络公司来说，核心产品与市场的契合度可以非常强。说白了，人们下载这款应用、它的传播方式、分发途径、邀请好友或发送快拍等行为，产品与市场的契合度有时会强到令人惊叹，以至于你甚至分不清是自己开发的产品推动了用户增长，还是反而拖了后腿——毕竟用户增长基本是自然发生的。（00:36:53）正因如此，公司有时会误导用户。用户会觉得自己所做的那些与主流观点相悖的举动其实是正确的，但实际上那些举动根本就是错误的。而Snap成功的关键在于持续创新，对吧？（00:37:17）对于Snap这样的公司来说，竞争异常激烈。社交网络本质上就是垄断平台，Facebook或其他社交平台完全有动机遏制Snapchat的增长势头，而且他们确实下了很大的功夫。Snap成功的秘诀在于其独特的团队架构。我从未见过类似的模式。我在多家公司工作过，但Snap的CEO是个极度以产品为导向的人，他本人就是设计师，还亲自组建了设计团队。这支设计团队仅有10到12人，即便公司规模达到了五六千人，团队规模依然很小。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh wow. At 6 or 6,000 employees. The design team was, you said how many, five or six people?
turns.zh: 哇哦。五六千员工，设计团队才10到12人？

turns.speaker: Gaurav Misra
turns.en: 10, 12 people.

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: 10, 12. And to add to that, there's no PMs really for a long time. That was before.
turns.zh: 没错。更重要的是，公司很长一段时间都没有产品经理。这是早期的情况。

turns.speaker: Gaurav Misra
turns.en: For a long time, yeah.
turns.zh: 是啊，那个时候确实没有。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Big difference.
turns.zh: 差别很大啊。

turns.speaker: Gaurav Misra
turns.en: Initially, there were no PMs at all. PMs were introduced with monetization. Once monetization was a big sort of element, that's where PMs came in. Today, I think there's a ton of, or there's an adequate number of PMs across the company, but there was a long period of time, especially when the innovation was happening, when there were a much, much smaller number of PMs and it was very designer led. But at the same time, I think that's slightly misleading in the way that these weren't your sort of average designers. (00:38:43): These were designers who were actually PMs as well. That's what the secret sauce was. They were able to not just design but also do the PM part which is a big responsibility. It's a lot of work, especially for that many employees, but it gave the CEO a way to have granular control over what exactly was being launched in which part of the app at all times. (00:39:05): Because he could meet with a set of 10 or 12 people and know every change that was happening that was user impacting. A lot of changes were being worked on that were infrastructure and types of things that keep going on in the back end where you're improving ranking and whatever that might be, performance and things like that. And those were not usually his concern. He was concerned with what UI are we adding where? And if you needed to add UI to the app, you needed it designed. And if there's no designers in the company, except for a handful who talk directly to the CEO, you create a very granular control over what's being launched in the company. So everything needed to be approved by Evan. If you hadn't approved it, it's not going out. So the design team actually held a lot of power in that.
turns.zh:
起初，公司根本没有产品经理（PM）。PM是随着商业化进程引入的。当商业化成为一个重要元素时，PM们才应运而生。如今，我认为公司内部PM数量充足，但在创新阶段，PM数量非常有限，设计师主导了产品开发。不过从某种角度看，这也存在误区——这些设计师并非普通设计师，而是同时兼任PM角色。这才是关键所在。他们不仅要设计产品，还要承担PM的重任。这对规模较大的公司来说压力巨大，但它赋予了CEO对产品发布节奏的精细把控权。

（00:38:43）CEO能与10到12人开会时，就能掌握所有影响用户体验的变更细节。许多后台优化工作（如提升排名、提升性能等）通常不在他的关注范围内。他专注于界面设计的落地位置。若没有设计师团队（除少数直接向CEO汇报的成员外），CEO对产品发布的把控就更加严密。所有变更都需经过Evan批准，否则无法上线。因此，设计团队在产品决策中握有实权。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This is awesome. So what I'm hearing partly is, I don't know if this is true, but it feels true that to make a consumer app that is successful and breaks through, you almost need a singular mind that continues to stay in the weeds on everything. And the way Evan did that is very close to the design team who basically ran product.
turns.zh: 这太棒了。所以我听到的部分观点是（不确定是否属实，但感觉确实如此）：要打造成功且突破性强的消费级应用，几乎需要一个能深入理解每个细节的核心人物。而Evan正是通过与设计团队紧密合作来实现这一点的，设计团队实际上在很大程度上负责了产品管理工作。

turns.speaker: Gaurav Misra
turns.en: That's very true. Yeah, it's very true. And he was able to keep the context of the entire app in his head at the same time. He knew the interdependencies and what we're doing and why we're doing it. And so that gave him just very granular control over the company's product roadmap.
turns.zh: 这太对了。是的，确实如此。他能同时将整个应用的上下文烂熟于心。他清楚各模块的相互依存关系、开发方向及背后的逻辑。这让他对公司的产品路线图拥有极高的把控权。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It makes me think about Brian Chesky and Airbnb is a consumer product, it's not a social network, but I wonder if that's just an interesting insight just for consumer products. They will generally do better if there's one person with a really ... the right sort of combination of experiences, insights, and just they continue to run and own every detail.
turns.zh: 这让我联想到布莱恩·切斯基和Airbnb。Airbnb是消费级产品，不是社交网络，但我好奇这是否仅是消费级产品的一个有趣特质。若有一位具备合适经验、洞察力，并能持续把控所有细节的人，这些产品通常会表现得更出色。

turns.speaker: Gaurav Misra
turns.en: Definitely. And also the ability to bring about change, the ability to truly energize an entire organization to do something that's not just incremental but fundamental. (00:40:58): << Founder mode >>
turns.zh: 确实如此。还有推动变革的能力，能够真正激发整个组织去开展那些不仅是渐进式的，而且是根本性变革的工作。（00:40:58）：《创始人模式》

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Exactly.
turns.zh: 没错。

turns.speaker: Gaurav Misra
turns.en: Founder mode. That's what we're getting to, basically.
turns.zh: 创始人模式。这就是我们要谈论的核心问题。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, ever heard of it. Okay. And then you said that these designers, so I know it's famous that Snap had no PMs for a long time. Designers were PMs. This point you made about the designers where PME is really important. I think a lot of people look at this, they're like, "Amazing. We're just going to hire just designers. We don't need all these PMs. Slow everything down. Just tell us what not to build." Can you just talk about the level of these designers? What allowed them to be as successful as they were without any PMs?
turns.zh: 是啊，你肯定听说过。好的。然后你提到这些设计师，我知道Snap很出名，长期没有产品经理，设计师自己充当产品经理。你提到的设计师在PME方面的重要性。我觉得很多人会想，"太棒了。我们就直接雇佣设计师好了。我们不需要那么多产品经理。放慢进度就行。只要告诉我们哪些功能不要做就行。"你能谈谈这些设计师的水平吗？他们是如何在没有产品经理的情况下取得如此成功的？

turns.speaker: Gaurav Misra
turns.en: Yeah, I mean I think what was expected from the designers now was not just the ability to design, the skill set of designing, which all of them were IC designers by the way. And there were no reports, so they weren't allowed to have reports actually. And so they were designing everything themselves, but they also had to have the leadership skills to go figure out the roadmap, write all the documents, work with the different teams, figure out shipping schedules and just know everything, not just the technical and the engineering part, but the UX and the UI and the product needs and why are we doing this. (00:42:15): The roadmap, there's just a ton to keep in mind. And that means that it was a job that was just highly ... it was very high workload. No doubt, very high workload. These people work really hard and they were paid highly too. For what it's worth, they were paid way higher than you would expect designers or PMs or engineers to be paid with quarterly bonuses and all kinds of things.
turns.zh: 是啊，我觉得现在对设计师的期望不仅仅是设计能力——毕竟他们都是内部设计师——而且他们没有汇报层级，实际上不允许有汇报层级。所以他们要自己设计所有东西，但同时还必须具备领导技能，规划路线图、撰写所有文档、与不同团队合作、确定发布时间表，掌握所有方面，不仅是技术和工程方面，还包括用户体验、用户界面、产品需求以及我们为什么要这么做。（00:42:15）：路线图需要考虑的因素太多了。这意味着这份工作的工作量极高……压力非常大。毫无疑问，压力非常大。这些人工作非常努力，薪酬也很高。如果你感兴趣的话，他们的薪酬远远高于你对设计师、产品经理或工程师的预期，还有季度奖金之类的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's interesting. And it reminds, people always say, "Why do you need PMs?" There's like someone has to do the work that a PM does. They're not sitting around doing nothing. And it's important to note the person that will take on the PME work, they have to be good at it and enjoy it. And a lot of designers don't want to be doing writing docs and organizing stakeholders and getting alignment and ...
turns.zh: 很有意思。这让我想到，人们总是问："为什么需要产品经理？"总得有人做产品经理的工作啊，他们又不是闲着的。需要注意的是，承担PME职责的人必须擅长这项工作，并且乐在其中。很多设计师不想负责撰写文档、协调利益相关方、达成共识等等……

turns.speaker: Gaurav Misra
turns.en: 100%, 100%. That's why it was so hard to find those people who were able to do two things. I actually think there's an insight in there is innovation between when you're merging craft right between two different functions. And I do think there's something special about one person doing two different functions or at least being able to do. And I think a lot of unique insight and innovation can come from that. (00:43:31): I actually think on my personal side, I eventually joined the design team. I started at Snap on the engineering team. I eventually joined the design team over the last two years that I was at Snap. And a big part of what I did there was create this function called design engineering. And that was actually a different combination. It wasn't the designer PM. It was the designer engineer. The person who can think of the UX design it and also build it and launch it, all of those things. (00:44:03): And we saw both the ability to take designers and teach them engineering and take engineers and teach them design as part of that. Obviously, the reason that we created that function was very different. It was actually to continue innovating as the company got bigger. One of the problems that we identified was that as the company got bigger and bigger and there's like 500 engineers, 1,000 engineers, 2,000 engineers, 3,000, suddenly it just becomes very difficult to do everything. (00:44:32): Everything is a six-month project or a one-year project. Every product is a massive investment of 500 engineers and a lot of time. And so you really have to pick your bets. If you get it wrong, if you are innovating and trying to create new products and you spend 500 engineers for a year and it doesn't work, it's a big problem. You're going to be in trouble, especially if we're coming like Snap where everybody was copying what they're doing so they had to constantly innovate, create new stuff and push the bounds. (00:44:59): I think Evan's philosophy was always he didn't fight the things that were getting copied, right? Stories got copied pretty much straight up. A lot of things that Snap created got copied, but he was more of the mindset of like, "Let's expand the pie, do something new and push the boundaries." We'll keep innovating basically. And so to do that with that scale of a company becomes really hard. And so we had this idea of let's create a small team where we can go and pretest a lot of these ideas because we had a lot of ideas and we can't go and build all of these things. So the idea was create a small team of these design engineers, people who are able to do the entire product design engineering process in their head and can put together early versions of the product, which we would actually bake into the Snapchat app itself. (00:45:46): And we were able to even test, for example, run a test in Australia, see how it's performing. Run a test in a couple of high schools, just a couple of high schools, see how people behave. And that way we already have data on how this might perform in a real world environment, but we haven't built it to production level. It's a prototype, essentially. It's how a startup might build something. (00:46:08): The same idea of what we're doing at our company now, build fast, get it out there, get feedback, understand whether it works or not, and then work with the engineering team to build it at a scale. Once we understand the product and the dynamics, then it makes sense to put on 500 engineers for six months to build it. (00:46:25): So that was a big part of it. I think the nice thing that came out of it that was completely unexpected but actually transformational for me in a way was obviously in big organizations, alignment is a big issue. How do you get everybody on the same page? And a big part of a PM's job is actually to create alignment and it can be a lot of work because you go talk to all these stakeholders and get them on the same page. (00:46:48): But one of the insights that we had, which was unique was as the company gets bigger, you can actually create alignment by causing internal virality. If there's enough people in the company, it actually starts acting like a consumer base might. If you share something interesting with someone, they will share it with somebody else because they think it's interesting and you can actually create virality inside a company. (00:47:16): So one thing that we would do is we would create these prototype products. We would just go into an area, redo a bunch of stuff, create these prototype products that didn't exist in Snapchat normally, and then we would just share the build and it would explode. It would just go viral inside the company. Day after day we would hear from engineers, then managers, then VPs, then eventually from Evan being like, "Oh my God, everyone's talking about this. Why am I the last one to hear about it?" (00:47:47): So it would create instant alignment across the company of this is exciting, this is something that we want to get behind. And everyone would be asking, "When are we doing this? When is this happening? I see someone's already working on it." So it was a great way to do that. And once we really understood that the product actually had good dynamics and we had tested it, it was a great way to get it out in front of everybody and create this idea of, "Hey, we're all working on this. This is the future."
turns.zh:
100%，100%。所以要找到能同时胜任两项工作的人才如此困难。我认为这其中蕴含着一个洞见——当你将两个不同职能的专业能力融合时，创新就会产生。我确实认为，让一个人同时胜任两个不同职能，或者至少具备这种能力，是非常特别的。我相信许多独特的洞见和创新都源于此。  
（00:43:31）：就我个人而言，我最终加入了设计团队。我最初在Snap的工程团队工作，过去两年在Snap期间，我转到了设计团队。当时我做的最重要的工作是创建了一个叫做“设计工程”的职位。这实际上是一种不同的组合，不是设计师兼任产品经理，而是设计师兼任工程师。即既能构思用户体验设计，又能亲自实现并推向市场的人。  
（00:44:03）：我们发现，可以把设计师培养成工程师，或者把工程师培养成设计师。这显然是出于不同的目的。我们的初衷是随着公司规模扩大，继续保持创新能力。当时我们发现的问题是，随着公司规模不断扩大，工程师从500人增长到1000人、2000人、3000人，很多事情就变得难以推进了。每个产品都需要500名工程师投入一年时间进行大规模开发。于是你必须有所取舍。如果方向错误，比如你创新新产品却失败了，那就是大问题。尤其是在Snap这样的公司，所有人都模仿我们的做法，所以必须不断创新、创造新事物、突破边界。  
（00:44:59）：我认为埃文（Evan）的理念始终是不与被模仿的东西抗争，对吧？Stories（故事功能）几乎被完全复制。Snap创造的很多东西也被复制，但他的思维是：“让我们扩大蛋糕，尝试新事物，突破界限。”我们基本上会持续创新。但在如此大规模的公司中做到这一点确实很难。因此我们想到了一个办法，组建一个小团队，在那里我们可以预先测试许多创意想法，因为我们有很多想法，但不可能全部开发出来。于是我们决定组建一个由设计工程师组成的小团队，他们能在脑海中完成整个产品设计工程流程，并能快速搭建产品原型，这些原型最终会被整合到Snapchat应用中。  
（00:45:46）：例如，我们甚至能在澳大利亚进行测试，观察其表现。或者在几所高中进行测试，仅限几所学校，观察用户行为。通过这种方式
我们已经掌握了这款产品在现实环境中的表现数据，但尚未将其提升至生产级别。说白了，这就是个原型产品——就像初创公司开发产品时常做的那样。（00:46:08）这与我们公司当前的运作思路如出一辙：快速开发、快速发布、收集反馈、评估成效，再与工程团队合作进行规模化开发。一旦我们深入理解了产品及其运行机制，再投入500名工程师、耗时六个月进行全面开发就顺理成章了。（00:46:25）这正是关键所在。让我意外且深受启发的是，在大型企业中，团队协作往往面临巨大的挑战——如何让所有人达成共识？而产品经理的核心职责之一就是协调各方意见，这项工作往往耗费大量精力——需要与各利益相关方反复沟通，最终达成共识。（00:46:48）但我们发现了一个独特的解决思路：随着公司规模扩大，通过内部传播机制也能实现协同效应。只要公司内有足够多的人员参与，内部传播机制就能模拟出类似消费者市场的行为模式——当你分享有趣内容时，人们会主动传播，因为这本身就具有吸引力。（00:47:16）我们的做法是创建原型产品。进入某个业务领域，重新设计一系列功能，推出Snapchat中原本不存在的原型产品。这些产品一经发布，便在公司内部引发热议。日复一日，工程师们、经理们、副总裁们，甚至Evan本人都会惊呼：“天哪，大家都在讨论这个！我怎么最后才知道？”（00:47:47）这能瞬间凝聚全公司的共识："这太令人兴奋了，我们必须全力支持！"每个人都会追问："什么时候开始开发？进展如何？我看到有人已经在推进了。"这种方式堪称妙招。一旦我们确认产品确实具备良好的市场潜力并完成测试后，再通过这种方式让全公司上下都参与进来，共同构筑"我们都在为此努力，这就是未来"的共识。

turns.en: Today's episode is brought to you by Coda. I personally use Coda every single day to manage my podcast and also to manage my community. It's where I put the questions that I plan to ask every guest that's coming on the podcast. It's where I put my community resources. It's how I manage my workflows. Here's how Coda can help you. （01:00:15）这款产品最终失败了，但它看起来像是TikTok推出前的早期版本。所以我觉得这在某种程度上是件好事，因为Snap确实有使命感，也在解决问题。不过我认为社交媒体现在出现了分野。传统社交媒体是和朋友分享内容，但想想过去那些应用如何走红的日子——你分享给朋友，朋友再分享给朋友，大家都纠结于如何通过朋友分享内容、如何发送消息等等。

（01:00:59）那个时代已经结束了。现在病毒式传播通过完全不同的机制实现——算法决定你的内容是否值得展示给任意数量的用户，这就是社交媒体的新时代。TikTok、YouTube Shorts、Instagram Reels等等都在践行这种模式。我认为这正在改变人们互动的本质，改变内容走红的根本机制。从监管角度来看，我们应该区别对待这两类产品。

（01:01:37）一方面是用户决定谁能看到内容，另一方面是公司决定内容呈现方式。这实际上是公司的声音。所以我不知道，第230条法律是否适用于这类产品？我真的不确定。或许我们思考问题的方式有误，这值得探讨。

turns.speaker: Gaurav Misra
turns.en: It's fundamental. At the end of the day, a time where video images, audio can't be trusted actually hasn't existed for a while. If you think about ... I mean there was a world in the 1800s where there was no video or audio or images and everything was proven by he said, she said for the most part. And it's possible that if everything can be generated and anything can be created and it looks just as real as if it were real and there's no way to tell, then we might actually return to that world where there's no way to prove anything besides physical evidence or he said, she said. (01:03:20): And I think that's scary, but also possibly opens a bunch of new opportunity for someone to figure out how to solve this problem. I think it's going to be a big problem. I do think today, we are almost there in terms of creating absolutely photorealistic video. I mean the very recent models, a very cutting edge is just about ... It feels like a few centimeters away from achieving it, but I do think to fully get there to the point where it cannot be differentiated at all, it's still a couple of years away. (01:03:52): I also think that it is use case driven in a way. I think thinking about Captions for a second, we take a unique view on what type of video we want to focus on. Video generation and text to video generation. If you look at it today, it's all silent video. There's no audio and it's often what you think of as stop video or B-roll, right? You can actually make a movie with B-roll. And a lot of a movie or a TV show or a social media post or an ad actually is dialogue or monologue. That's actually what it is is people talking to each other, to the camera, interacting. That's actually what makes true story. (01:04:35): B-roll is supportive elements that are showing up to set the scene or something like maybe before the scene opens, you see a few shots of New York City or LA or something, and then you jump into the room and now two people are talking. So our goal is to solve the talking video problem. How do we create video where people are delivering dialogue or monologue or things like that? And that's what we focus on purely. And there actually isn't a lot of work happening in that area today and it's not a solved problem. We're getting there, we're getting closer and closer, but today's models actually bifurcate a little bit. (01:05:15): So there's a set of companies today that are able to create these types of what we're talking about is avatar videos. They're using this technology called neural rendering. It's actually not a technology that's affected by the transformer and diffusion model revolution or the large model revolution, essentially. This is a technology that existed separately and it doesn't have anything to do with the AI growth happening right now. It just happens to produce semi-realistic outputs, but it actually stops at some point because it's not clear how it becomes generalizable in every situation. (01:05:55): It has to be trained on people individually. So you might ingest a little bit of video of you and then you can generate you. And so it's a different technology and a different outcome, essentially. And a bunch of companies using this type of model, a bunch of companies are doing general text to video with no audio today. These are large generative models and they have the capability to do more, but that frontier just hasn't been reached yet. I think there's no doubt in anybody's mind on the research side that it is 100% solvable. It's just like somebody has to go do it and we haven't gotten there yet. Nobody has had the time to go and do that yet. So that's where we're at, essentially. (01:06:35): We're working purely on large generative models for talking videos. So that's our core focus. I do think though, from a safety perspective, we have a unique framework or how we think about it. So generally videos divide into two categories. So for us, we think on one side of what is documentation, so this is the type of video that it could be a personal video where you're taking a video with your friends and you're hanging out, you're at a restaurant. It's documenting what happened. You had fun, whatever it was, it's for your memories. And there's a non-personal version of this which is like, oh, it's like a reporter documenting a crime or something that happened or whatever it is and who was involved, where was it? Maybe it was a natural disaster or something, and this is for history. We want to see what happened. (01:07:27): And there's actually no benefit to AI-generated video in any of this. Actually, all of this, it's just negative. It's all negative. If we are generating fake versions of reality to fool people, there's just nothing good about that. And we want to stay away from that, essentially. We want to design products and build products that make it difficult to use for that particular use case, for anything that falls within that. And on the other side, you have what we think of as storytelling. (01:07:56): Now this could be ads, it could be social media posts, it could be TV, movies. All of these things are storytelling. They're designed for entertainment, they're designed for fun. And nobody believes if you watch a Geico commercial, you're not thinking that the gecko is real selling insurance somewhere out there. You know that this is fabricated and it's for entertainment. And same with reality TV even, right? It's called reality TV. It's definitely not reality and social media, ads, all this stuff falls in the category. (01:08:28): And if we can enable more people to tell stories and entertain other people and get their message out there, that is pure positive. This is where we want to focus. And a lot of our effort in the product and design process goes into how do we design products and build products that specifically make it really hard to use on one side and really easy to use on the other side. And that's the real challenge.

这至关重要。说到底，在当今这个视频图像和音频无法被轻易证实的时代，其实已经持续了一段时间了。如果你回想一下……我是指19世纪的世界，那时没有视频、音频或图像，一切都主要靠道听途说来证明。若一切都可以被生成、随意创造，且看起来和真实无异，却又无法辨别真伪，那么我们或许会回归到那个只能通过实物证据或口头陈述来证明一切的世界。（01:03:20）：我认为这很可怕，但同时也为人们解决这个问题带来了新的机遇。我认为这将是一个重大挑战。如今，我们在创建极其逼真的视频方面几乎达到了极限。我是说最近的模型，处于前沿阶段，感觉距离实现还差几厘米，但要达到完全无法区分真假的水平，可能还需要几年时间。（01:03:52）：我认为这在很大程度上是由应用场景驱动的。以字幕为例，我们对视频类型有独特的定位——视频生成和文本转视频生成。如今的视频大多是无声的。没有音频，通常被视为过渡镜头或B-roll素材，对吧？你甚至可以用B-roll素材制作电影。很多电影、电视剧、社交媒体帖子或广告实际上都是对话或独白——人们互相交谈、对着镜头互动，这才是真正的故事。（01:04:35）：B-roll是辅助元素，用来设定场景。比如在场景开始前，你会看到几张纽约或洛杉矶的镜头，然后切入对话场景。所以我们的目标是解决对话视频问题。如何创造出人们进行对话或独白的视频？这才是我们专注的重点。目前这领域研究不足，尚未解决。我们正在不断接近目标，但现有模型存在分野。（01:05:15）：如今有一些公司能制作我们所说的虚拟形象视频。他们使用一种叫做“神经渲染”的技术。这项技术本质上不受Transformer和扩散模型革命或大模型浪潮影响。它是一个独立存在的技术，与当前AI热潮无关。它能生成半真实的输出，但在某些情况下会遇到瓶颈，因为如何让其在所有场景下通用化仍存疑问。（01:05:55）：这项技术必须
这些模型是基于单个人的训练数据。因此，你可能会输入一段自己的视频片段，然后就能生成你的虚拟形象。从本质上讲，这是一项完全不同的技术，产生的结果也截然不同。目前有很多公司在使用这类模型，但大多数都只专注于无声文本转视频的应用。这些大型生成式模型本有更强的功能，但目前尚未完全开发出来。研究界普遍认为这一技术100%可行，只是尚未有人去实现它——毕竟这需要耗费大量精力。  

（01:06:35）：我们目前专注于用于会说话视频的大型生成式模型。但从安全角度来看，我们的思路独树一帜。视频通常分为两类：一类是记录型视频，比如朋友聚会、餐厅用餐等日常生活片段，记录下当时的场景和回忆；另一类是非记录型视频，比如新闻记者记录犯罪现场、自然灾害等事件，这些属于历史记录范畴。  

（01:07:27）：在这些应用中，AI生成的虚假视频毫无益处。相反，所有此类应用都存在负面影响。如果我们用虚假视频欺骗公众，那绝非善举。因此，我们致力于设计产品，阻止此类用途。  

（01:07:56）：另一类应用是故事性内容，比如广告、社交媒体帖子、电视节目和电影。这些都是为娱乐而设计的。观众看Geico广告时，绝不会相信那只壁虎真的在卖保险。他们知道这只是虚构的场景，用于娱乐。真人秀节目也是如此，它们本质上并非真实生活。  

（01:08:28）：如果我们能让更多人讲好故事、娱乐大众、传播信息，这才是真正的积极贡献。这才是我们努力的方向。我们在产品设计中投入大量精力，确保产品在不同场景下呈现出截然不同的体验：一方面难以被滥用，另一方面易于被正确使用。这才是真正的挑战。

turns.en: It comes back to what we were talking about before where the reality is that no matter how interesting, advanced and amazing a technology is, science fiction has become reality. And people are just like, "How did you get so good at writing?" And they're not telling anybody, but there's still a ton of people who don't even know that these advancements have happened. And so adaption is actually much slower, even for the most exciting things. Of course, in tech circles, everybody's talking about it, but the reality is it takes a while to get out there. (01:11:33): And I think for companies that are going to succeed, they're going to have to figure out how to market these products so that they can be the ones to reach all these people that have the problems that they're now able to solve. And we think about that every day. So on that note, as a consumer product, we spend a bunch of time and money on marketing our products, and we often use performance channels and all kinds of things, but about a year ago, we would run AI video in ads and things like that, and we would get all these comments of people being like, "Oh my God, this is so fake. Don't show me this." (01:12:08): And around that time, the technology got just about good enough that suddenly, those comments stopped happening and suddenly, you could get performance that was even better than actually recording with a person because you could just try more things. 这又回到了我们之前讨论的观点：现实情况是，无论一项技术多么有趣、先进和令人惊叹，科幻小说终究会成为现实。我们当时就谈到这一点。电视上那些曾经的科幻桥段，如今已然成为现实，而大多数人甚至都还不知道这件事。（01:11:01）：我的父母住在印度，他们是附近唯一了解ChatGPT的人，他们用这些词汇为社区写下了令人惊叹的笔记。人们会问：“你是怎么写得这么好的？”他们并未向任何人透露此事，但仍有大量人甚至不知道这些进步成果已经出现。因此，即便是最激动人心的事物，普及速度也往往非常缓慢。当然，在科技圈里，大家都在谈论它，但现实是，要让它真正普及需要时间。（01:11:33）：我认为，要想成功的公司必须找到推广这些产品的有效方法，这样才能触达那些正面临着他们能够解决的问题的群体。我们每天都在思考这个问题。因此，作为消费品公司，我们在产品营销上投入了大量时间和资金，经常使用效果广告渠道等手段。但大约一年前，我们在广告中使用AI视频时，用户留言称：“天哪，这太假了，别给我看这个。”（01:12:08）：大约在那个时候，技术水平终于足够高，突然间，这些负面评价消失了。你可以获得比真人拍摄更优质的效果，因为你可以尝试更多可能性。你可以生成30到40种创意，其中一种就能胜出，而且胜出的创意比真人拍摄的还要出色。更有趣的是，当涉及本地化时，你需要将内容翻译成每种语言。一旦你找到成功的创意，现在你还得为每个市场进行本地化处理，从头开始重建。（01:12:51）：这实在是太耗费精力了。很多时候效果并不理想，因为本质上是重新思考了整个过程。但我们发现，用AI翻译后的效果几乎和原文一样好。这项技术必将席卷整个市场。我认为，只要能创造或节省利润，它就必将普及。它会迅速在社交媒体上风靡一时。（01:13:21）：你可以想象未来的社交网络——顺便说一句，这听起来很反乌托邦，所以大家要注意了。你可以想象未来的社交网络，所有内容都是生成的。没有真实用户。算法不再根据用户喜好定制内容，而是完全为你量身打造内容，用户和一切都完全迎合你的需求。我认为
这根本不可能。虽然某种程度上这几乎不可避免，但我觉得这还为时尚早。说实话，这很可能在五年左右就会成为现实。
